note: The native looks: Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets, and the iOS Live Activity, as data (shared/types/nlook.ts). Change it, raise v by one, and phones take it at their next open. Every design here is a BUNDLED DEFAULT that draws what today's native views draw, so a phone that holds nothing else still has something to fall back to that is not blank. The server cleans every design on publish, the phone cleans again before writing, and native code clamps a third time; anything unknown, too new, too big or broken draws the hand-written native view instead. v NEVER repeats: the server keeps a high-water mark, so a rollback re-serves under a higher number.

ink.note: The app's own palette (experience/bots/palette.ts), white and ink with greys. THE one source: it replaces the widgets.look literals, iOS X0Palette and Android WidgetInk. The legacy widgets.look knob is a CHECKED COPY of these colours, not a generated one (defaults.ts stays import-free): legacyLookOf(palette) in experience/native/catalog.ts rebuilds it and a test deep-equals the two, so drift fails the build. The knob keeps its own shape and does not gain dim, outline or hollow. Colour belongs to bots alone ($color), never to the frame.

island.note: The Dynamic Island is always black, whatever the phone's appearance. Both schemes are the same on purpose.

dusk.note: The evening palette: the same ink and white, settled down. Deeper ground, a softer rule, a little more air between the greys. Still NO colour of its own — colour belongs to bots alone ($color), never to the frame — so a dusk design on a tinted or Always-On screen degrades exactly as an ink one does.

x0.plain.note: The end of every widget fallback chain: a name and one line, in nothing but palette roles, with the bot whose card it is beside the name when a card is shown. It fits every family and can never be over a limit, so a phone always has somewhere to land before it gives up and draws the native view.

x0.base.note: What today's X0 widget draws, as data: it leads with whatever matters most (a question, a job, the last thing done, else the greeting), exactly as X0Widget.swift and TailzuX0Widget.kt do. Accessory roots draw only the glance's own lock words, never a question's.

bots.plain.note: The end of the Live Activity fallback chain: the bot's name and the stage, in roles only. Each region a design does not hold falls back on its own to today's hand-drawn region, so this is only ever a last resort for a region that IS named.

bots.base.note: What today's "Bots at work" draws, as data: the Lock Screen banner and every island region (BotsActivity.swift). A question's words are marked sensitive, so on a locked phone they are redacted and the lock-safe fill is used instead — the same rule activity.ts already applies to the alert.

x0.dusk.note: THE EVENING FACE of the X0 widget, and the first design that is a design rather than today's view written down. Three things make it its own: the bot is a STILL from the bots' own catalog (drawn on the phone, so it keeps that person's colours and nothing personal is sent anywhere to render it), a drawn horizon sits behind everything as the one piece of furniture, and the lead line is set in `display` rather than `brand`. It leads on the same four cases as x0.base, because what matters most does not change with the hour. Accessory roots stay on the glance's own lock words: a question never goes on a Lock Screen in full.

x0.slab.note: NUMBERS FIRST. The second real design, and deliberately the opposite of x0.dusk: no art and no drawn picture beyond the card's own bot (its dotted still, or its face when it asks) — one big count, one caption, one rule and a line of words. It exists to prove the cheap end of the format works as well as the rich end: every root here is text, a rule and at most one small bot, so it costs almost nothing to decode, it draws identically in tinted and Always-On modes, and it is the design to reach for when a phone is tight on memory. The count is `counts.needs` when something waits and `counts.working` when something is running, chosen by `if` rather than by arithmetic, because format 1 has no arithmetic.

bots.night.note: THE LIVE ACTIVITY AT NIGHT. The island is always black whatever the phone's appearance, so this design is dark by definition rather than by choice. Three differences from bots.base: the banner leads with the running timer at a size you can read across a room, the stage list is drawn as its own row of names rather than only as a bar, and the island's bottom region carries the ETA from `vars` when the server has one (a free string the frozen ContentState has no field for, and the reason `vars` exists). Every region missing here falls back on its own to today's hand-drawn one, region by region.

board.night.note: A BOARD for the spare "X0 Board" kind, in the evening palette: the week as beads, the count that waits, and the people's faces under a rule. The board kind is an AppIntentConfiguration whose one parameter picks which board to show, so a second board is a design in this catalog, never a second widget kind — and a shipped widget kind can never be removed, which is why there is exactly one. It falls back to board.base, the bundled default that keeps the kind from ever being empty at review or on first run (App Review 2.3.1).

bu.base.note: Android's ongoing "Bots at work" notice: a template fill, not a canvas, because Android 16 Live Updates refuse custom layouts. The chip is what the status bar and Always-On show, so it binds only non-sensitive paths; the notice is posted VISIBILITY_PRIVATE with a public version built from this same lock-safe fill.

board.base.note: The bundled default board for the spare "X0 Board" kind, so that kind is NEVER empty at review or on first run (App Review 2.3.1). A shipped widget kind can never be removed, so this design must keep working for as long as the kind exists. The medium's second column is ONE line: words.working is already "{n} working", so a count above it would read "3" over "3 working". That line stays at 12pt and the row aligns "end" ON PURPOSE, so it sits on the "Needs you" caption's baseline and the needs count stays the only big number; at 34pt it would crowd out week.line in longer languages. The row is wrapped in a V with a trailing Spacer so it sits at the TOP on both platforms (SwiftUI would otherwise centre it in a fill-height frame), and the H carries w:fill so its Spacer can push week.line to the right edge on Android.
